ch01.note: Iga, and its neighbour Kōga just across the passes in Ōmi, were the two districts of central Japan most closely tied to the shinobi — the spies and infiltrators for hire later romanticised as ninja. The whole world of the novel rests on this.

The nineteenth year of the Tenshō era: 1591. By this date Toyotomi Hideyoshi had all but completed the reunification of Japan begun by Oda Nobunaga. The novel keeps the old lunar calendar, on which the third month falls in spring.

A shaku is about 30.3 cm, so the staff runs to roughly 2.1 metres. The novel keeps the Japanese measures throughout — length (shaku, sun), distance (ri, chō, ken), yield (koku) — and glosses each at first use rather than converting it.

御斎峠, on the border of Iga and Ōmi and one of the seven passes leading out of the Iga basin. The name is usually read Otodo-tōge; Shiba gives it the softer reading Otogi (‘fairy tale’) that titles the chapter.

Tōyaku (当薬) is the dried herb Swertia japonica, ferociously bitter and a common folk remedy for the stomach. The old man's antique, dialect phrasing, and this rustic kindness, are what mark him to the woodcutter as a stranger from elsewhere.

The Tenshō Iga War. Nobunaga's son Nobukatsu invaded Iga in 1579 and was thrown back; in 1581 (Tenshō 9) Nobunaga invaded again and destroyed the province's warrior-league — the calamity that hangs over the whole novel. The event and its date are well attested. Shiba's figure of ‘more than twelve thousand’ Oda troops (given later in the chapter) is a modest one; modern estimates of the second invasion run as high as forty to sixty thousand.
A chō (also written 町) is about 109 metres.
Rappa (乱波) is an eastern-Japanese word for a shinobi: a spy, scout and saboteur for hire. Shiba uses rappa, shinobi and ninja for the same men.

Jizamurai, literally ‘samurai of the soil’: minor warriors who worked their own land and served no lord. In Iga they governed themselves through the sworn league the passage goes on to describe, and it was from their households that the ninja came.

In the sixth month of Tenshō 10 (June 1582) Nobunaga's own general Akechi Mitsuhide turned on him and killed him at the Honnō-ji, a temple in Kyoto. Nobunaga's ally Tokugawa Ieyasu, caught nearby at Sakai with only a handful of men, escaped home by exactly the secret route across Iga described here — the celebrated ‘divine lord's crossing of Iga.’

In 1571 Nobunaga stormed and burned Enryaku-ji, the great Tendai monastery on Mount Hiei above Kyoto, killing thousands. With his massacres of the militant Ikkō Pure-Land leagues at Ishiyama and Nagashima, it stands for his war on independent religious power — the hatred of the irrational Shiba makes of him in this passage.

The ichinomiya, or first shrine, of Iga province. The old chronicles record that when Nobunaga toured the conquered province late in 1581 and rested here, surviving Iga men led by Otowa-no-Kido fired on him with matchlocks and missed, killing only his guards. The episode is traditional rather than firmly documented.

A koku (about 180 litres of rice) was reckoned a year's food for one person, and a domain's worth was measured in koku. A stipend of a few thousand made these Sakai tea-merchants the equals of minor lords.

Sen no Rikyū, the supreme master of the tea ceremony, here under his lay name Sōeki; with Imai Sōkyū and Tsuda Sōgyū he was one of Hideyoshi's three tea masters. There is a quiet anachronism in the naming: Jirōzaemon speaks of Rikyū as a living stipendiary, but Hideyoshi had ordered him to commit suicide on the twenty-eighth of the second month of this very year, Tenshō 19 — a month before the scene, which is set late in the third.

ch01.anchor: the foot of the Great Buddha
ch01.note: The rendezvous is at the foot of the great bronze Vairocana of Tōdai-ji in Nara, the colossus of the old southern capital. Its hall had burned in 1567 in the fighting between Matsunaga Hisahide and the Miyoshi (see the following chapter), and in 1591 the Buddha still sat roofless and open to the weather, its head crudely patched; it would not be housed again until the eighteenth century. This is not the newer Great Buddha that Toyotomi Hideyoshi was then raising at the Hōkō-ji in Kyōto.
A gatha (偈) is a Buddhist verse or hymn; the sunset gatha (日没偈) is one chanted at nightfall as part of the daily temple office.

ch01.anchor: at the Hour of the Ox
ch01.note: The old day was divided into twelve two-hour periods, each named for an animal of the zodiac and counted from the Rat at midnight. The Hour of the Ox fell roughly between one and three in the morning: the rendezvous is set for the dead of night.

ch02.anchor: But there was no hall over it.
ch02.note: The colossal bronze Buddha of Tōdai-ji in Nara, and the “rain-soaked Buddha” of the chapter's title. Its hall had burned in 1567 (see below), and for well over a century the Buddha sat out in the open, exposed to sun and rain, until a new hall was finally raised in 1709.

Matsunaga Hisahide (1508?–1577), a byword in Japanese memory for treachery, rose from obscurity to rule Yamato; Danjō was his court title. In the tenth month of 1567 (Eiroku 10), during his war with the Miyoshi Triumvirate (a coalition of three Miyoshi captains then contesting the Kinai), his forces fired the hall in which the enemy had entrenched, and the Great Buddha burned with it. He later defied Oda Nobunaga and, besieged in 1577, is said to have destroyed himself and a prized tea-caddy rather than surrender.

The Tamon-in nikki, the diary kept by successive heads of the Tamon-in, a cloister of the great Nara temple Kōfuku-ji, is a major eyewitness chronicle of these years; the quoted passage records the burning of the Great Buddha Hall. The diarist calls the image a Shakya, the historical Buddha, though the Tōdai-ji colossus is in fact a Vairocana.

Aizen Myō-ō (Rāgarāja) is a fierce, red-bodied Buddhist “wisdom king” who turns worldly passion into the energy of enlightenment; he was invoked as a patron of love, and by extension by those whose living depended on it. His image, set in the ruined hall, shadows the chapter's crossing of desire and killing.

A bahan ship was a pirate-trader of the sort manned by the wakō, the Japanese-and-continental sea-raiders who preyed and traded along the China coast and beyond. Luzon, the northern Philippines, had just come under Spanish rule from Manila; Korea would be invaded by Hideyoshi the following year. That a hired thug had ranged such waters marks how far Japan's violent men now reached.

Takeda Katsuyori (1546–1582), last lord of the Takeda of Kai, the great cavalry house broken by Nobunaga and Ieyasu; hunted down, he died in 1582. Shiba's point is that Iga men served the Takeda and their Tokugawa enemies at once, keeping up contact across the lines—his emblem of the Iga spies as a guild loyal only to their own trade. The anecdote is the author's; take it as characterization rather than documented fact.

ch03.anchor: the foxes come out as early as the fourth hour
ch03.note: In Japanese folk belief the fox is a shape-shifter that takes human form to trick travellers, and dusk is its hour. Jūzō's joke is aimed at the tall woman who appeared and vanished a moment before: in a port rich enough to draw the whole world, he says, even the foxes are out early. The “fourth hour” of the old night-reckoning is about ten in the evening.

Late-medieval Sakai was the wealthiest port in Japan and all but self-governing, run by a council of its great merchants and ringed by moats and gates like a free city; Europeans likened it to Venice. In Tenshō 11 (1583), building his castle at Ōsaka, Hideyoshi ordered the merchants to move there and had Sakai's defensive moats filled in, ending its independence. The “eight years” since sets this scene in 1591.

ch03.anchor: Sōkun—that would be the son of Imai Sōkyū
ch03.note: Imai Sōkyū (1520–1593) was one of the three great tea masters of Sakai, alongside Sen no Rikyū and Tsuda Sōgyū, and the arms-merchant who bankrolled first Nobunaga and then Hideyoshi. This chapter tells his story; that he is Jūzō's paymaster was established in the first chapter.

法印 (Hōin, “Seal of the Law”) is the highest of the priestly ranks of the Buddhist clergy; from medieval times the court also conferred it, and the lesser 法眼 (Hōgen, “Eye of the Law”), as honorary titles on eminent laymen—physicians, artists, and men of great wealth. Sōkyū's titular court office was 大蔵卿 (Ōkurakyō, Minister of the Treasury); with the Hōin rank it made him “Ōkurakyō-Hōin.” His rival Konishi Ryūsa held the parallel Izumi-Hōgen. The chapter's title, “The White Hōin,” is Sōkyū, in his white robe.

関白 (Kampaku), Imperial Regent, was the highest civil office of the court and the source of Hideyoshi's authority to rule in the Emperor's name; he took it in 1585. “The Kampaku,” “that lord of the realm,” and Hideyoshi are one man throughout the chapter.

Takeno Jōō (1502–1555), the Sakai merchant who did most to shape the austere wabi style of the tea ceremony, and the teacher of Sen no Rikyū. To have studied under him set Sōkyū at the centre of Sakai's tea world.

A katatsuki (“shoulder-blow”) is a shouldered ceramic caddy for powdered tea. Under Nobunaga and Hideyoshi the great named tea-utensils were prized above castles and granted as rewards for whole provinces; Nobunaga made a deliberate policy of collecting them. The Matsushima caddy was among the most famous of all, and presenting it to Nobunaga is what launched Sōkyū.

In 1568 Nobunaga marched on Kyoto and installed Ashikaga Yoshiaki as the fifteenth and last Ashikaga shogun—the move that opened his bid for national power. At that date he held Owari and Mino (the novel adds Suruga, which was not in fact yet his) and was still only one warlord among many, his eventual dominance far from assured.
天下布武, “spread military rule over the realm”: the motto Nobunaga stamped on his seal from 1567, declaring his purpose to unify Japan by force.
A kin (catty) is a weight of about 600 grams, so thirty kin is roughly eighteen kilograms of gunpowder.

ch03.anchor: the Great Buddha of the Hōkō-ji
ch03.note: This is Hideyoshi's own colossal Buddha, a lacquered wooden image begun in 1586 for his Hōkō-ji temple in Kyoto—not the ancient bronze Buddha of Nara that the earlier chapters describe. It was meant to outdo the Nara Buddha and to display the wealth of the new regime.

ch03.anchor: the ruin of the Western Army at Sekigahara
ch03.note: The battle of Sekigahara (1600), won by Tokugawa Ieyasu over the “Western Army” of Hideyoshi's loyalists, decided the succession and founded the Tokugawa shogunate. The narrator's aside—that Ryūsa would fall with the Western Army “nine years after this”—fixes the present scene in 1591. Konishi Yukinaga, named here, was among the Western commanders executed after the battle.

北政所 (Kita-no-mandokoro), the title of the principal wife of a Regent—here Hideyoshi's wife, born Nene—who wielded real influence at court and in his household. That Ryūsa's wife served as her secretary shows how far the Konishi had risen inside Hideyoshi's inner circle.

From 1591 Hideyoshi openly prepared to invade Korea as the road to conquering Ming China; the first armies crossed in 1592, and the campaigns would grind on for six years and end in failure. For a Sakai merchant living on the China and Korea trade, the war meant the closing of his markets—Sōkyū's motive for wanting Hideyoshi dead.

ch03.anchor: his one son, Tsurumatsu, is dead
ch03.note: Tsurumatsu, Hideyoshi's only son, died in the eighth month of 1591, not yet three years old—within days of the scene here. With no direct heir, Hideyoshi adopted his nephew Hidetsugu and made him Kampaku; but Hidetsugu commanded little loyalty, and Hideyoshi would force him to suicide in 1595. The child's death is the crack in the Toyotomi settlement that Jūzō points to.

南蛮, “Southern Barbarians,” was the Japanese name for the Europeans—Portuguese and Spanish—who reached Japan by sea from the south in the sixteenth century, and for their goods. “Nanban iron” is imported European iron, prized for firearms and fine metalwork.

ch04.note: Hōka-sō (放下僧): itinerant entertainer-monks of medieval Japan, half-priest and half-mountebank, who juggled, tumbled, spun tops and performed sleight of hand at roadsides and festivals. The crowd on the riverbank has gathered to watch just such street performers.

A low mountain among the eastern hills of Kyoto, rising beyond the Kamo river. Its western slope is Daimonji-yama, later the site of the giant character dai (大, “great”) traced in bonfires above the city each August for the Bon festival of the dead. Kisaru points the crowd at its peak to sell them the phantom storm-cloud.

ch04.anchor: Gion was not yet a quarter of teahouses
ch04.note: Gion, the district below the Yasaka Shrine on the east bank of the Kamo, became in later centuries Kyoto’s most famous pleasure-and-teahouse quarter, the haunt of the geisha. Shiba’s aside reminds the reader that in 1591 none of that yet existed: the road ran through farmland and temple ground.

Katō Kiyomasa (1562–1611), one of Hideyoshi’s foremost generals, holder of the court title Governor of Higo (Higo-no-kami) and lord of a great fief in Kyushu. That an Iga man who had entered his open service was hunted down and killed by his own former comrades shows how the shadow-clans policed the ones who left them for a lord’s pay.

Maeda Gen’i (1539–1602), a former Buddhist priest who rose to become Hideyoshi’s governor of Kyoto—the office the text calls the magistracy of the capital. He policed the city, oversaw its temples and shrines, and ran the web of informers that watched for spies and men of doubtful business: the very service Gohei has now entered under a false name. Gen’i later sat among Hideyoshi’s Five Commissioners of state.

ch05.note: A rakshasa (Japanese rasetsu) is a flesh-eating demon of Indian and Buddhist myth, absorbed into Japan as a figure of the man-devouring ogre. The valley's name recalls the legend told just below: a demon that fed on the corpses of women and, when there were none, came down into the city to seize the living.

ch05.anchor: the burial ground of one sovereign after another
ch05.note: The Sennyū-ji, a temple in the eastern hills of Kyoto, has served since the thirteenth century as the mortuary temple of the imperial house; the tombs of many emperors from Shijō (reigned 1232–1242) onward lie within its grounds. The eerie bridge, and the guide's talk of crossing out of the world of the living, play on this: the road climbs toward the imperial dead.

Hattori Hanzō (1542–1596), the most celebrated of all Iga ninja, served Tokugawa Ieyasu; in 1582, after Nobunaga's death, he guided Ieyasu to safety across the mountains of Iga. He commanded Ieyasu's Iga and Kōga men, and the Hanzō Gate of the later Edo Castle still carries his name. His role here as the broker between the Tokugawa and the Iga gōshi is historical.

Hideyoshi twice staged spectacular hand-outs of gold and silver, in 1585 and 1589 (the thirteenth and seventeenth years of Tenshō), heaping the metal at his Jurakudai palace and dealing it to nobles and warlords. The display of wealth was itself an instrument of rule. The totals Shiba cites are of the order reported by contemporaries, though such figures cannot be verified exactly.

The Jurakudai (‘Mansion of Assembled Pleasures’) was Hideyoshi's vast palace-fortress in the capital, completed in 1587 and pulled down only a few years later, in 1595. It gives the following chapter its title.

The kōshin cult, of Chinese Daoist origin, kept a sleepless night-long vigil on the eve of each kōshin day of the sixty-day calendar; its guardian emblem was the monkey, most often carved as the three ‘see no evil, hear no evil, speak no evil’ figures. To crouch like a carved kōshin monkey is to be still, hunched, and mute.

ch06.note: A kunoichi is the ninja's cant word for a woman agent, made by breaking the single character for 'woman' (女) into the three strokes that compose it—ku, no, ichi. The lines that follow give the shadow-world's view of her without softening it: a woman was trained and spent as a tool, fed a counterfeit love and never loved in return, on the creed that a ninja keeps himself whole only by keeping his heart pitiless.

ch06.anchor: hidden writing used only by ninja
ch06.note: Shinobi-moji, 'shadow writing': a secret syllabary by which ninja passed dispatches among themselves, and from which the chapter takes its title. Several such ciphers survive in the ninja manuals; the scheme described here—forty-nine signs, one for each syllable of the old iroha alphabet, each built from a left element (the five elements, plus man and body) and a right one (six colours)—belongs to that family. Its use is social as much as practical: only another of the trade could read it, so the mere fact that the note comes in cipher tells Gohei that its sender knows what he is.

Kashima, in the eastern province of Hitachi, and its sister shrine Katori across the river were revered as the twin cradles of Japanese swordsmanship, and the classical fencing schools traced their descent to them. The tradition's most famous son, named a little further on, was Tsukahara Bokuden (1489–1571), reckoned the supreme swordsman of his age and sword-teacher to the shogun, who likewise rose from the Kashima shrine-families.

Miyamoto Musashi (c. 1584–1645), the most storied swordsman in Japanese memory and author of the Book of Five Rings. His feud with the Yoshioka—a hereditary fencing house of Kyoto, one of the 'eight schools of the capital'—is the stuff of legend. Shiba's aside looks ahead: in 1591 Musashi was still a child, and his Kyoto duels lay more than a decade in the future.

ch06.anchor: a face like the goddess Kisshōten's
ch06.note: Kisshōten (from the Indian goddess Lakshmi), the Buddhist deity of beauty, fortune, and abundance; her name is a stock figure for a beautiful woman.

ch07.note: Hōrai (Chinese Penglai) is the mythical island-mountain in the eastern sea where, in Daoist and Japanese lore, the immortals dwell amid palaces of jewel and gold; a stock emblem of paradise and unearthly splendour. Shiba invokes it for the strange, otherworldly silhouette of the Jurakudai’s tower.

ch07.anchor: Konishi Yukinaga, Settsu-no-kami, lord of Uto
ch07.note: Konishi Yukinaga (c. 1555–1600), like his father Konishi Ryūsa a Sakai merchant’s son (the family traded in medicines), rose through Hideyoshi’s favour to become a daimyō, lord of Uto in Higo. In 1592 he did lead the First Division — the vanguard — across to Korea, exactly as the street-talk here anticipates; a Christian convert (baptised Agostinho), he was executed after Sekigahara (see the note at that name in ch03). That a former tradesman should privately dread the war he would be made to lead is consistent with the record. Corroborated.

ch07.anchor: the mother of the Korean king Sŏnjo
ch07.note: Sŏnjo (Japanese reading Senso; r. 1567–1608) was the reigning king of Chosŏn Korea, upon whose realm the coming invasion would fall. The tale that Konishi’s house was secretly in league with a “mother Hei” of the Korean king is Shiba’s own invented rumour, and the narration at once calls it groundless; only the king’s name is real. Uncorroborated, and presented as false.
Tenjiku (天竺) is the old Japanese name for India, and by extension the farthest edge of the known world. Paired here with Luzon in the Philippine islands, it means simply “to the ends of the earth.”

Kohagi quotes a proverb — nobori ongyoku, kudari heihō, “music comes up from the capital, swordsmanship goes down from the east” — pairing the refinement of the Kamigata (the Kyoto–Ōsaka region) with the martial prowess of the eastern provinces, Azuma, the Kantō, home of the Kashima and Katori sword traditions (see ch06).

ch08.note: Makuzugahara was a moor at the western foot of Higashiyama, on the eastern edge of the capital, long celebrated in poetry for its hagi, or bush-clover. Dew on its autumn clover is a set seasonal image; here the line is traded at the crossroads as a greeting that marks the turn toward autumn.

Ishida Jibu-no-shōyū is Ishida Mitsunari (1560–1600), the ablest of Hideyoshi’s civil administrators, here bearing the court title Jibu-no-shōyū (Junior Assistant in the Ministry of Ceremonies). After Hideyoshi’s death he led the western daimyō against Tokugawa Ieyasu and was defeated and executed at Sekigahara in 1600. He becomes a central figure late in the novel.

In 1582, when Oda Nobunaga was killed at the Honnō-ji, Hideyoshi wheeled his army back from his western campaign and crushed the assassin, Akechi Mitsuhide, at Yamazaki, between the capital and Ōsaka. The victory set him on the road to mastery of the realm; it is that ‘keen edge’ the passage remembers.

The go-bugyō: five senior administrators Hideyoshi set over the civil government of the realm. Maeda Gen’i and Ishida Mitsunari were both among them. After Hideyoshi’s death the board fell out among itself, and its rivalries fed the war that ended at Sekigahara.
Yanagimachi was the licensed pleasure-quarter of the capital in this period, forerunner of the later Shimabara. Its brothels and their courtesans are the ‘quarter of wine and women’ Jūzō drifts into.

ch08.anchor: came running from the hills and fields of Iga to guard him
ch08.note: This is the famous ‘crossing of Iga’ (Iga-goe): on Nobunaga’s murder in 1582, Ieyasu, caught near Sakai with only a small escort, fled home to Mikawa over the mountains of Iga and Kōga, guided and shielded by local ninja under Hattori Hanzō. The escape itself is historically attested; the figures tradition attaches to it—the seventy-eight men, the two hundred, the thousand kan—are less firm. It is the root of the Iga men’s loyalty to the Tokugawa.

ch09.anchor: guardian deity of the Buddhist way
ch09.note: Marishiten is the Japanese form of Mārīcī, a Buddhist deva of Indian origin who personifies the mirage and the shimmer of heat (Sanskrit marīci, a ray of light). Because she is said to go unseen before the sun, she was invoked for invisibility and for protection in danger, and from the medieval period she was widely revered by warriors — and, in ninja lore, by the shinobi of Iga and Kōga. The words Gen'i chants over the scroll are her shingon, or true-word invocation. It is her Kōga cult that supplies the byname behind the chapter's title, “Mari of Kōga.”

ch09.anchor: the Udaifu wiped the Iga men out
ch09.note: The Udaifu (from 右大臣, Udaijin, Minister of the Right, an office he held from 1577) is Oda Nobunaga; the men of Kōga name him by his court title. His invasion and near-extermination of the Iga ninja in 1581 is the Tenshō Iga War, noted earlier; he was himself killed at the Honnō-ji the following year.

The Naifu (from 内大臣, Naidaijin, Inner Minister) is the court title by which Tokugawa Ieyasu came to be known, and by which contemporaries and later histories alike refer to him. Dōgen's reading — that the great lords are quietly hedging toward Ieyasu against the day the Toyotomi fall — anticipates exactly the realignment that would produce the battle of Sekigahara in 1600.

ch09.anchor: the daughter of the lord of Odani
ch09.note: This is Yodo-dono (Chacha), eldest daughter of Azai Nagamasa, lord of Odani castle in Ōmi, and Hideyoshi's favourite consort. The dead child is their son Tsurumatsu (noted earlier), who died in 1591 at the age of two and whose loss unbalanced the ageing Hideyoshi. The “another son” Dōgen foresees would be Hideyori, born in 1593, whose birth did indeed reopen the succession crisis Dōgen here predicts.

A real figure: Rokkaku Yoshikata (later styled Jōtei), of the Sasaki-Rokkaku house, hereditary military governors of southern Ōmi and long the overlords the Kōga men served. Nobunaga broke the house in 1568, taking its stronghold of Kannon-ji castle as he marched to install a shogun in Kyoto; Yoshikata took the tonsure and lived out his years in obscurity. His fathering of Kohagi, and her adoption by Imai Sōkyū, are the novel's invention hung upon this real history.

In 1487 the ninth Ashikaga shogun, Yoshihisa, marched in person against Rokkaku (Sasaki) Takayori and encamped at Magari in Ōmi. The Kōga men, fighting for Takayori by stealth and night-raid, harried the shogunal camp for months on end; Yoshihisa sickened and died there in 1489 without ever taking his enemy. The feat made the name of the Kōga shinobi, and this campaign is the historical kernel of their fame.

ch09.anchor: The fifty-three houses of Kōga, they say
ch09.note: The “fifty-three houses of Kōga” (Kōga gojūsan-ke) is the traditional name for the confederation of warrior-farmer families of the Kōga district, who governed their own affairs by council rather than under a single lord and hired out their skill in stealth-warfare. The number, and the roll that follows, come from later Kōga records; the families were real, though the list is best read as tradition rather than exact register.

ch09.anchor: Kōga Saburō is a monstrous figure
ch09.note: Kōga Saburō is the hero of a widely-told medieval legend, bound up with the origin-tales of the Suwa shrine: betrayed and cast into an underworld, he wanders for years, returns transformed into a serpent or dragon, and is at last enshrined as a god. Kōga tradition took him for the founding ancestor of its ninjutsu. The tale is folklore, not history.

ch09.anchor: Oiro Tayuya, the spy of Prince Shōtoku
ch09.note: By a parallel legend the Iga trace their art to a shinobi who served Prince Shōtoku (574–622), the great early patron of Buddhism, as a spy. Like the Kōga Saburō tale this is a founding myth rather than record; Shiba sets the two side by side to point up the rivalry of the neighbouring provinces.

Hideyoshi's siege of Odawara in 1590 destroyed the Later Hōjō, the last great independent power in the east, and completed the unification of Japan under him. With no more war to fight at home, the demand for ninja fell away — which is why, as the narration observes, Dōgen finds his fellow Kōga men idle.

Not the famous castle of Owari, but the Nagoya castle in Hizen (modern Saga prefecture, at the north-west tip of Kyūshū): a vast fortress and camp-town thrown up in 1591–92 as the muster-point and headquarters for the invasions of Korea. Hideyoshi directed the war from here.

ch10.anchor: that open way was the usual method
ch10.note: The two modes of ninja infiltration: the open way—going in by daylight or by open force, bluff and disguise—and the shadow way of stealth by night (in the ninja manuals, yōnin and innin). Against another ninja the open assault is the safer choice, noisier but leaving the attacker's back covered, which is why Jirōzaemon's fatal change of mind, from the open way to the stealthy one, is the hinge of the scene.

The midsummer Buddhist festival of the dead, held in the seventh lunar month (the same festival marked by the Daimonji bonfires noted earlier): the spirits of the ancestors are believed to return to the household and are seen off again with lights on the final night. The whole capital is thus abroad after dark tending its dead—cover for Jirōzaemon, and the source of the scene's ghostly cast.

Shōchū is a clear distilled spirit, far stronger than fermented rice wine. Jūzō wants it to pickle the severed hand in a cask before the trophy is carried back to its owner at the magistrate's mansion.

The flight runs east out of the capital, making for the ninja country. Higashiyama is the range of hills that walls Kyoto on the east; the riders cross it by the Shibutani pass, drop past the temple town of Daigo and down the valley of the Uji river, and by daybreak are among the hills of Kōga—the province of the Kōga ninja, which borders Iga.

ch11.note: The infant name of Hideyoshi's son and heir, the future Toyotomi Hideyori, born to Yodo-gimi in the eighth month of Bunroku 2 (1593). He was called Hiroi — literally foundling, a child picked up off the ground — because an elder son, Tsurumatsu, had died small; a baby of doubtful luck was by custom pretended to be abandoned and then “found” again, to cheat the spirits that steal infants away.

Taikō is the title of a retired kampaku, the civil regent of the emperor. Hideyoshi took it in 1591, when he resigned the regency to his nephew and adopted heir Hidetsugu, and it is the name by which he is most often remembered. Jūzō means that the day they fix upon to kill him in the coming seventh month will forever after be kept as the Taikō's death-anniversary.

The Makasōgi-ritsu, the monastic code of the Mahāsāṃghika school of early Buddhism, rendered into Chinese in the early fifth century by the Indian monk Buddhabhadra (359–429), who worked in the south under the Eastern Jin. A vinaya lays down the rules of conduct for the ordained; the lines that follow name the standard divisions of moral action — the three sins of the body (killing, theft, unchastity) and the four of the mouth (the double tongue, abuse, the lie, and idle talk). That a guild of assassins should keep the first of these precepts, and only while preparing a killing, is the irony Shiba draws out.

Jitō (reigned 686–697), the female sovereign whose reign closes the Nihon Shoki. In her third year (689) the court proclaimed certain waters and moors — among them a moor in Iga — grounds where the taking of life was forbidden, an early edict in the Buddhist spirit. Shiba offers it, half in earnest, as a possible root of the Iga ninja's peculiar attachment to the one precept against killing.

Her given name is written with the character for a hanging reed blind, ren; the name everyone actually uses, Kisaru, is written “tree-monkey” and means something like little monkey. The nickname — half fond, half mocking — was her dead father Jirōzaemon's, as she lets slip a moment later.

Jūzō and Kohagi trade the word keshō (化生), a Buddhist term for a being born not from a womb but by sudden transformation — one of the four modes of birth, the manner ascribed to gods, demons, and the dwellers in the hells. In common Japanese it came to mean an apparition or shape-changer with no fixed, true form. Jūzō uses it of the ninja who, trained from childhood, has hollowed out his own self and become whatever the moment demands; here he means it as the highest praise of Kohagi's art.

ch12.note: Yoshino, a mountainous district south of Nara, has been celebrated since ancient times for its cherry blossoms—tens of thousands of trees planted over the centuries on the slopes around the temple of Kimpusen-ji. A spring pilgrimage to view them was already a national institution; Hideyoshi’s progress here in the spring of 1594, with a suite said to number some five thousand, was among the most lavish flower-viewings ever staged.

Maeda Toshiie (1538–1599), one of Hideyoshi’s oldest comrades-in-arms and most senior generals, lord of the great domain of Kaga on the Japan Sea. After Hideyoshi’s death he was for a time the one man able to hold the balance between the Toyotomi loyalists and the rising Tokugawa Ieyasu.

This came to pass in 1595, the year after the flower-viewing. Hidetsugu (see the earlier note on him) was accused of plotting treason and ordered to take his own life; his severed head was then set up at the Sanjō riverbed in Kyoto, and there his women and children—more than thirty in all—were beheaded in public before it. The purge cleared the succession for Hideyoshi’s infant son Hideyori.

The Zaō-dō, the towering main hall of Kimpusen-ji, the temple at the summit of Yoshino and a chief center of Shugendō, the cult of the mountain ascetics. It enshrines the fierce guardian Zaō Gongen, and its monks held authority over the whole mountain.

A hut on a Yoshino peak associated with Saigyō (1118–1190), a warrior who abandoned his rank to become a wandering monk and one of Japan’s most beloved poets. His verses on the cherry blossoms of Yoshino made the place a byword for the beauty and the impermanence of the flowers.

Noh is the masked, slow-paced classical dance-drama of medieval Japan, chanted to flute and drums; its performers were organized into hereditary schools, of which the Kanze school was the foremost. A takigi-nō is Noh played outdoors at night by the light of bonfires—a form descended from the sacred torchlight Noh staged each spring at the Kōfuku-ji temple and Kasuga shrine in Nara. In a Noh play the shite is the principal, often a god or a spirit; the waki is the secondary role, usually a traveling priest or courtier who witnesses the shite’s revelation, and may be attended by one or two wakizure companions.

The play is Yoshino Tennin (“The Celestial Maiden of Yoshino”), a real work of the Noh repertoire. A tennin—in Sanskrit an apsaras—is a celestial being of Buddhist cosmology, a heavenly dancer who dwells in the paradises of the Buddha and descends to the human world; here one appears among the cherry blossoms of Yoshino to reveal her true form in dance.

The only surviving copy of the book, the scan from which this translation was made, lacks a single leaf at this point—its printed folios 404 and 405. Roughly two pages of the original are therefore lost: the nightly thieving of the dance from the Kanze house, and the beginning of the night of the performance. Nothing has been invented to bridge the gap; the translation resumes exactly where the readable text does, in mid-sentence.

A small whistle blown to imitate an owl’s hooting, by which ninja signaled one another in the dark without drawing notice. The novel takes its title, Owl’s Castle, from the owl as the emblem of these creatures of the night.
A sasumata is a two-pronged iron fork on a long shaft, used to pin a man by the neck or a limb and take him without killing him—the standard implement for capturing an armed opponent alive.

ch13.note: Mimi means ‘ear’: a by-name the man earned from his famously keen hearing, of which he boasts later in the scene. Nabari is a town in the province of Iga, in the heart of the ninja country.

The kozuka is the small utility knife carried in a slot on the scabbard of a sword, its blade only a few inches long. It is with this that Kuroami makes the man pin his own hand to the floor — a test not of skill but of the one thing he prizes in a ninja, the power to rise above pain.

Kuroami is working a counter-spell against the illusion Mimi has laid on him, out of the esoteric-Buddhist lore the ninja borrowed. He first knots the Samaya hand-sign of the bodhisattva Samantabhadra — one of the ritual finger-interlockings, or mudrā, of the tantric schools — breathes into it, and recites a protective formula; then he ‘cuts the nine signs,’ the kuji: nine slashing strokes, five level and four upright, drawn in the air with two fingers to seal off evil, a practice shared by the mountain ascetics and the ninja. The chanted lines echo the old sutra-tag shichinan sokumetsu, shichifuku sokushō, ‘the seven calamities at once destroyed, the seven blessings at once brought forth.’

ch13.anchor: a castle on the hills of Fushimi
ch13.note: Hideyoshi’s castle at Fushimi, on the hills just south of Kyoto, was begun in 1592 as a retirement seat and rebuilt on a grander scale after an earthquake threw it down in 1596. It became his last residence and the place of his death in 1598; the struggle for the succession that followed runs through the rest of the book, which ends at Fushimi Castle.

ch13.anchor: the early Genki and Tenshō years
ch13.note: The Genki (1570–1573) and Tenshō (1573–1592) eras: the height of the wars of unification, when the country was still broken enough that a ninja could find ready work everywhere. It was late in this span, in the Tenshō Iga rising of 1581, that Nobunaga — here called by his court title, the Udaifu — smashed the ninja province.

The chapter’s title, Suiku (水狗), reads literally ‘water dog.’ Shiba names several of his sections with such emblems rather than plain titles, and the force of this one gathers only here, at the close: the aged rappa who hunted by night lie strewn and half-drowned along the bed of the river, like so many dead dogs washed up at the water’s edge.
